title: An uncertainty-versus-temperature plot asks whether a smooth curve can honour the few values an expert reported
summary: A rate coefficient's uncertainty factor is reported at a handful of temperatures. A smooth function of temperature is needed everywhere in between. The plot overlays the reported values (dots) with a smooth construction (green) and a literature version (red), and shows where they agree and where a smooth form cannot follow the data.

media.alt: Uncertainty factor f from 0 to 0.4 against temperature from about 200 to 2500 K. A green curve and a red dashed curve fall steeply from 0.3 near 220 K to a minimum near 0.08 at 350 K, then follow a shallow wave near 0.1 up to 1000 K and rise almost linearly to 0.3 at 2000 K. Blue dots mark reported values: 0.3 at the two ends and 0.1 from 300 to 1000 K.

read_the_figure.question: Does the smooth uncertainty function reproduce the reported uncertainty values at every temperature, and where does it deviate?
read_the_figure.axes: x: temperature in kelvin, from a few hundred to 2000 or 2500 K. y: uncertainty factor f, from 0 to 0.4. Blue dots: values reported in the source tables. Curves: smooth functions built to match them (legend names).
look_at: Dots versus curve. Where a curve passes through or near a dot, the construction reproduces that reported value.
The bowl shape. All curves have a minimum at intermediate temperature and rise towards both ends: the uncertainty is smallest where the data are best.
In figure 18 (R4) the green and the red curves almost coincide, and both pass through the reported values at the ends (0.3) and in the middle band (0.1).

In figure 19 (R5) the dots form a step: a low plateau, then a high plateau, then a middle plateau. A single smooth curve cannot follow steps. The green and black curves stay between 0.15 and 0.21 and miss the high plateau, while the red dotted curve has a dip at the cold end and a hump in the middle.
Which curves are labelled with a different suffix (MUQc, Rxn5m): they are variants whose differences from the base curve are tiny where the lines overlap.
read_the_figure.proves: That a smooth uncertainty function reproduces the reported values at the ends and in the middle where the table is simple, and quantifies where it cannot (stepped values). It does not show the physical uncertainty is that smooth.
if_wrong: A curve that dips below zero or has an extra wave: the functional form has too many degrees of freedom for the data.
A curve that misses a plateau of dots: the form cannot represent a step, so either change the form or accept the error.
Two curves that differ only where there are no dots: the difference is the modelling choice, not data.
A curve at the exact dot values only: it is interpolating, not constructing an uncertainty function.
must_check: The definition of f is stated (log10 of a factor, or a relative range).
What the dots are: reported values, with a reference.
The temperature range of the curves and of the data.
All curves in the legend are explained.
The y axis label is spelt correctly (it is not here).

terms.meaning: A temperature-dependent measure of how far a rate coefficient may lie from its nominal value. In many combustion databases it is the log10 of the largest allowed ratio.
The uncertainty assigned to a rate coefficient before using any new data in a fit.
A formula that gives f at every temperature from a few parameters, instead of a table of values.
The matrix describing the spread and correlation of the three Arrhenius parameters.
A temperature range in which the reported f is constant.
An interpolation passes through every reported value. A fit does not need to, and the difference is the residual.
A factor of 10 to the power f, so f = 0.3 is about a factor of two.

remember: A smooth function with three parameters cannot follow an arbitrary table.
f in log10 units: f = 0.3 is a factor of 2, f = 1 a factor of 10.
The curve is smallest where the data are best.
Dots are reported values, not measurements.
Differences between curves are modelling choices.

steps.title: The log rate coefficient is linear in three parameters
steps.note: Same representation as in the Arrhenius-curves figures of this group: ln k is linear in (ln A, n, E_a/R).

steps.title: Variance of the log rate coefficient
steps.note: If the parameters have covariance Sigma, the variance of the curve at T is a quadratic form in theta. This is the generic result for propagating a covariance through a linear map.

steps.title: The curve is the square root of a quadratic form
steps.note: Because Sigma is a covariance (positive semi-definite), the standard deviation g is never negative. Because Sigma has only six free numbers, g(T) has a limited family of shapes: typically one bowl. Steps and multiple plateaus cannot be reproduced exactly.

steps.title: Matching reported values
steps.note: The reported values f_j at temperatures T_j are targets for the construction, with c a convention constant that depends on how f is defined and on how many standard deviations the limits represent. The figure does not state c.

steps.title: Fit of Sigma to the targets
steps.note: With J greater than six targets the problem is overdetermined and residuals appear: the dots the curve misses are the residuals of this fit. With three or fewer distinct values it can be exact.

steps.title: From f to a factor
steps.note: Under the log10 convention f = 0.1 is a factor 1.26 and f = 0.3 is a factor 2.0. If the paper's f is defined differently, the factor changes: check the source.

worked.title: Converting plotted f values to factors
worked.problem: Assuming f = log10(k_max/k0), what rate-coefficient factor corresponds to the plateau values f = 0.1, 0.15 and 0.2 read from figure 19?

solution.text: Raise ten to the power f.

worked.answer: The rate coefficient may deviate by a factor of about 1.26, 1.41 and 1.58 from its nominal. The stepped plateau of 0.3 would be a factor of 2.0. The factors depend on the log10 convention, which the figure does not state.

analyze.q: Why does the green curve in figure 19 miss the 0.3 plateau between 1100 and 1700 K? Which property of the construction makes it unable to follow?
analyze.hint: Steps need more degrees of freedom than a three-parameter covariance has.

analyze.q: The red and green curves in figure 18 are almost identical. What does that say about how much the result depends on the particular construction for this reaction?
analyze.hint: The shape is determined by the data at the ends and the middle.

analyze.q: The red dotted curve in figure 19 dips at the cold end and rises in the middle. Is that a feature of the chemistry or of the construction?
analyze.hint: Remember there are no dots between 300 K and 1000 K except at 0.15.

evaluate.q: If the reported uncertainty steps from 0.2 to 0.3 to 0.15, should the smooth curve be forced through the steps or smooth over them? State the cost of each.
evaluate.hint: Over-confidence versus fidelity to the source.

evaluate.q: What extra information would you need before relying on the factor-of-two reading of f = 0.3?
evaluate.hint: Definition of f and the number of standard deviations.

create: Redraw the plot with the reported values as horizontal bars covering the temperature range over which each was stated, so the plateaus are visible, and shade the residual between curve and bar.
Design a construction that can follow a step: what is the minimum additional degree of freedom you would add to the three Arrhenius parameters?

checks.q: Why is the curve at intermediate temperatures lower than at the ends?
checks.hint: Think about where the data are.
checks.answer: The uncertainty of a rate coefficient is smallest where the underlying data constrain it best, in the middle of the measured range. Extrapolating to cold or hot temperatures amplifies the effect of the temperature-dependent parameters and the band widens.

checks.q: If f = log10(k_max/k0) and f = 0.3, how much larger can the rate be than nominal?
Why can a three-parameter covariance not follow a stepped table?
checks.answer: A 3 by 3 covariance has six free numbers, and the standard deviation along theta(T) is the square root of a quadratic form in (1, ln T, -1/T). That family has smooth bowls, not steps.

checks.q: Two curves match the dots equally well but one is much higher in the gaps between dots. Which is better?
checks.answer: Neither can be judged by the dots. The higher curve is more conservative and the lower more confident. The choice should follow the purpose: a conservative prior is safer for propagation.

checks.q: How would you test a smooth construction against a stepped table in a fair way?
checks.answer: Fit the construction on all plateaus except one, and compare its value on the left-out plateau with the reported one. If the miss is large, the form is too stiff for the data.
